faq.q: Why are simple partial seizures called focal aware seizures now?

exam: A 7‑year‑old presents with brief left‑hand jerks while remaining alert – what is your immediate diagnostic priority? — Obtain a focused seizure history and arrange neuroimaging to look for a focal lesion.
How does a focal aware seizure differ from a focal impaired‑awareness seizure? — The former preserves consciousness; the latter includes altered awareness or post‑ictal confusion.
A child with frequent focal seizures has a normal CT scan – what is your next step? — Request MRI if available; if not, refer for specialist imaging while treating any reversible metabolic cause.

Why is carbamazepine preferred over phenobarbital for focal seizures in children? — Carbamazepine has higher efficacy for focal onset and fewer sedative side‑effects; phenobarbital is less effective and can worsen cognition.
What red‑flag feature would prompt urgent referral to a tertiary centre? — Development of secondary generalisation or new focal neurological deficit.

A child with focal seizures lives in a malaria‑endemic area; what infection should you specifically screen for? — Cerebral malaria and neurocysticercosis; obtain malaria smear and cysticercosis serology.
Explain why correcting hypoglycaemia can stop focal seizures. — Low glucose reduces neuronal excitability thresholds, precipitating focal discharges; normalising glucose removes the trigger.
What distinguishes a psychogenic nonepileptic event from a focal aware seizure? — Lack of stereotyped EEG changes, variable presentation, and often associated psychosocial stressors.
ai.title: Focal Aware Seizure
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Focal aware seizures are brief episodes of motor, sensory, autonomic or psychic phenomena without loss of consciousness. They often herald structural brain disease and require targeted investigation in low‑resource settings.

b: Phenomena may be motor (e.g., jerks), sensory (e.g., tingling), autonomic (e.g., flushing) or psychic (e.g., déjà vu)
sections.p: A focal aware seizure is a seizure that starts in one cerebral hemisphere and does not impair awareness. Diagnosis is clinical, based on a stereotyped event described by the child or caregiver.

t.b: What was the exact sequence of symptoms? – Confirms focal onset and preserved awareness, distinguishes from generalized seizures
What does the video show? – Provides objective evidence of motor signs and helps localise the focus

b: Moderate: frequent (≥1/week) or brief impairment of school performance
Severe: daily events, secondary generalisation, or progressive neurological deficit
sections.p: Severity is judged by frequency, duration, impact on development and presence of secondary generalisation.

b: Post‑infectious scarring (cerebral malaria, neurocysticercosis, tuberculous meningitis)
sections.p: In low‑resource African settings, structural lesions are the commonest trigger; infections and metabolic disturbances are also frequent.

b: Motor: rhythmic jerks of a hand or face
Psychic: déjà vu, fear, auditory hallucination
sections.p: Children may describe or be observed having brief, repetitive movements, tingling, visual flashes or strange smells while remaining fully alert.
Goal: identify an underlying structural or metabolic cause; choose tests that are feasible locally.

t.b: What structural abnormality is present? – Detects lesions such as calcified cysticerci, tuberculoma, infarct; if unavailable, refer for imaging when possible
Are there reversible metabolic triggers? – Abnormalities guide immediate correction
Is HIV infection contributing? – Positive result prompts evaluation for opportunistic CNS lesions

t.a: Serology for malaria, cysticercosis, TB (where endemic)
t.b: Is an infectious cause likely? – Positive serology supports targeted antimicrobial therapy

b: Signs of raised intracranial pressure (vomiting, papilledema)
sections.p: Certain features suggest imminent danger or need for urgent referral.

b: Treat infections (e.g., antimalarials, anti‑TB drugs, praziquantel for cysticercosis)
First‑line ASM in children: carbamazepine or levetiracetam – chosen for efficacy in focal seizures and relatively safe profile
Avoid phenobarbital as monotherapy in focal seizures due to lower efficacy and sedation
Monitor for drug interactions (e.g., carbamazepine with antiretrovirals)
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; then use antiseizure medication (ASM) only if seizures are frequent or disabling.

b: Repeat imaging if seizures recur or new deficits appear
Vaccination and malaria prophylaxis to reduce infection‑related triggers
Counselling on safe sleep position and injury prevention
sections.p: Regular review to assess seizure control, growth, and drug tolerance; educate families on trigger avoidance.
